original-en.context: CANTERBURY. It must be thought on. If it pass against us, We lose the better half of our possession: For all the temporal lands, which men devout By testament have given to the Church, Would they strip from us; being valu’d thus: As much as would maintain, to the King’s honour, Full fifteen earls and fifteen hundred knights, Six thousand and two hundred good esquires; And, to relief of lazars and weak age, Of indigent faint souls past corporal toil, A hundred almshouses right well supplied; And to the coffers of the King beside, A thousand pounds by th’ year. modern-en.context: CANTERBURY. It must be considered. If it passes against us, we lose more than half of what we own. They would strip from us all the secular lands that devout men have left to the Church by their wills. The valuation runs like this: enough to maintain, for the King's honor, a full fifteen earls, fifteen hundred knights, and six thousand two hundred good squires; and for the relief of lepers and the weak elderly—those poor faint souls past physical labor—a hundred well-supplied almshouses; and into the King's coffers besides, a thousand pounds a year. That's how the bill runs.

original-en.context: CANTERBURY. Then hear me, gracious sovereign, and you peers, That owe yourselves, your lives, and services To this imperial throne. There is no bar To make against your Highness’ claim to France But this, which they produce from Pharamond: _In terram Salicam mulieres ne succedant_, “No woman shall succeed in Salic land;” Which Salic land the French unjustly gloze To be the realm of France, and Pharamond The founder of this law and female bar. Yet their own authors faithfully affirm That the land Salic is in Germany, Between the floods of Sala and of Elbe; Where Charles the Great, having subdu’d the Saxons, There left behind and settled certain French; Who, holding in disdain the German women For some dishonest manners of their life, Establish’d then this law, to wit, no female Should be inheritrix in Salic land; Which Salic, as I said, ’twixt Elbe and Sala, Is at this day in Germany call’d Meissen. Then doth it well appear the Salic law Was not devised for the realm of France; Nor did the French possess the Salic land Until four hundred one and twenty years After defunction of King Pharamond, Idly suppos’d the founder of this law, Who died within the year of our redemption Four hundred twenty-six; and Charles the Great Subdu’d the Saxons, and did seat the French Beyond the river Sala, in the year Eight hundred five. Besides, their writers say, King Pepin, which deposed Childeric, Did, as heir general, being descended Of Blithild, which was daughter to King Clothair, Make claim and title to the crown of France. Hugh Capet also, who usurp’d the crown Of Charles the Duke of Lorraine, sole heir male Of the true line and stock of Charles the Great, To find his title with some shows of truth, Though, in pure truth, it was corrupt and naught, Convey’d himself as the heir to the Lady Lingare, Daughter to Charlemain, who was the son To Lewis the Emperor, and Lewis the son Of Charles the Great. Also, King Lewis the Tenth, Who was sole heir to the usurper Capet, Could not keep quiet in his conscience, Wearing the crown of France, till satisfied That fair Queen Isabel, his grandmother, Was lineal of the Lady Ermengare, Daughter to Charles, the foresaid Duke of Lorraine; By the which marriage the line of Charles the Great Was re-united to the crown of France. So that, as clear as is the summer’s sun, King Pepin’s title and Hugh Capet’s claim, King Lewis his satisfaction, all appear To hold in right and title of the female. So do the kings of France unto this day, Howbeit they would hold up this Salic law To bar your Highness claiming from the female, And rather choose to hide them in a net Than amply to imbar their crooked titles Usurp’d from you and your progenitors.

modern-en.context: CANTERBURY. Then hear me, gracious sovereign—and you peers, who owe yourselves, your lives, and your service to this imperial throne. There is no obstacle to your Highness's claim to France except this, which they cite from Pharamond: _In terram Salicam mulieres ne succedant_—"No woman shall succeed in Salic land." This Salic land the French unjustly gloss as the realm of France, and Pharamond as the founder of the law and of this bar against females. Yet their own historians faithfully affirm that the Salic land is in Germany, between the rivers Sala and Elbe. There Charlemagne, having subdued the Saxons, left certain French settlers behind. Disdaining the German women for some loose habits, they established this law: no female should inherit in Salic land. That Salic, as I said, between the Elbe and the Sala, is today in Germany called Meissen. So it's clear the Salic law was not devised for the realm of France; nor did the French even possess the Salic land until four hundred and twenty-one years after the death of King Pharamond, who is supposed—idly—to have founded this law. He died in the year of our redemption 426; and Charlemagne subdued the Saxons and settled the French beyond the river Sala in the year 805. Besides, their own writers say that King Pepin, who deposed Childeric, made his claim and title to the crown of France as heir general, being descended from Blithild, daughter of King Clothair. Hugh Capet too, who usurped the crown from Charles Duke of Lorraine—sole male heir of the true line and stock of Charlemagne—to give his title some show of truth (though in pure fact it was corrupt and worthless), traced himself as heir to Lady Lingare, daughter of Charlemain, who was the son of Lewis the Emperor, and Lewis the son of Charlemagne. King Lewis the Tenth too, sole heir to the usurper Capet, could not keep his conscience quiet wearing the crown of France until he was satisfied that the fair Queen Isabel, his grandmother, was lineal descendant of Lady Ermengare, daughter to Charles, the said Duke of Lorraine. By this marriage the line of Charlemagne was reunited to the crown of France. So that, as clear as the summer sun: King Pepin's title, Hugh Capet's claim, King Lewis's satisfaction—all rest on right and title through the female line. So do the kings of France, even to this day; though they would hold up this Salic law to bar your Highness from claiming through the female, and would rather hide themselves in a net than openly defend their crooked titles, usurped from you and your forefathers.

modern-en.context: CHORUS. Thus with imagined wings our swift scene flies, in motion no less speedy than thought. Suppose that you have seen the well-equipped king at Hampton pier embark his royalty, and his brave fleet with silken streamers fanning the young sun. Play with your fancies, and in them behold ship-boys climbing on the hempen rigging; hear the shrill whistle that brings order to confused noise; behold the canvas sails, borne by the invisible creeping wind, draw the huge hulls through the furrowed sea, breasting the lofty surge. O, just imagine you stand on the shore and behold a city dancing on the unsteady waves—for so appears this majestic fleet, holding its true course to Harfleur. Follow, follow! Grapple your minds to the stern of this navy, and leave your England, still as dead midnight, guarded only by grandfathers, babies, and old women—either past or not yet come to full strength and vigor. For who is the man, with his chin just touched by one visible hair, who will not follow these select and choice-drawn cavaliers to France? Work, work your thoughts, and in them see a siege. Behold the cannon on their carriages, with fatal mouths gaping at girded Harfleur. Suppose the ambassador from the French comes back and tells Harry that the King offers him Katherine his daughter, and with her as dowry some petty and unprofitable dukedoms. The offer doesn't please; and the nimble gunner now touches the devilish cannon with his linstock,
